pages.text:
*The Handbook of Small Truths, Entry 17: Courage is a checklist you complete while shaking.*

Harbor smelled of roasted chestnuts and the sharp, metallic tang of brass instruments being tuned. Strings of amber lights crisscrossed the rim streets, casting long shadows that stretched and snapped in the gentle rhythm of the spin. Four thousand people moved through the air with a lightness that felt, to Kess, like a held breath finally released. She had spent the morning in the Council Hall, watching the vote pass, and now her ears still rang with the quiet satisfaction of a problem solved.

She found Lio where she suspected he would be: on the roof of the public library, sitting on the edge with his legs dangling over the drop into the crowded street below. He wore his navy flight-deck jumpsuit, the orange stripes on his shoulders bright against the twilight, and his black mag-boots were planted firmly on the metal grating. He was not looking at the dance. He was looking at his hands.

Kess sat down beside him, the gravel crunching softly under her white sneakers. She did not say hello. She did not ask if he was enjoying the festival. She simply reached into her tool-belt, pulled out a small, crumpled biscuit that she had stolen from Pim’s pocket, and broke it in half. She held one half out to him.

Lio looked at the biscuit, then at her, then back at his hands. The brass band had started a waltz, the notes drifting up from the street like bubbles rising through water. Lio took the biscuit. He did not eat it. He just held it, his fingers curled around the edges, his knuckles white against the crumbly surface.

"You look like you're trying to solve a differential equation with your thumbs," Kess said.

Lio’s mouth twitched, a faint, fragile line. "I am," he said, his voice dry and flat, stripped of its usual easy confidence. "It is a complex one."

"Can I help?"

He shook his head, a slow, deliberate movement. "Not yet. I am still collecting the variables."
pages.image: Kess in a green coverall sits beside Lio in a navy jumpsuit on a rooftop, holding a broken biscuit, while Lio stares at his hands; strings of amber lights and a busy festival street glow softly in the background.

pages.text:
It was not the wrenching of the bolts, nor the pressure of the suit, nor the sterile, humming silence of the airlock. It was the moment after the hatch swung open, when the vacuum was there, cold and absolute. There was no floor under his boots, no wall to his left, no ceiling above. Just the stars, which were not above, but all around, and underneath, and everywhere at once.

Lio set the biscuit down on the metal grating. He picked at a loose thread on his sleeve, his movements precise and mechanical. "I have been an EVA apprentice for two years," he said. "I am the best one aboard. I can fly a drone through a needle’s eye while correcting for Coriolis drift. I can replace a valve with my eyes closed. But I have never told anyone that I am afraid."

Kess leaned back on her hands, looking up at the dark curve of the drum’s interior, the stars visible through the glass panels above. "Afraid of what?"

"The no-down," Lio said. The words came out quick and sharp, like a valve slamming shut. "When I let go of the hatch frame, my brain expects a floor. It expects gravity to catch me. But there is no catch. There is only the fact that I am floating. And if I let go of the tether, I do not fall. I drift. And drifting is slow. And space is patient."

He looked at her, his dark eyes wide and unblinking. "I have been hiding it for two years. I tell myself it is just nerves. I tell myself it is part of the job. But it is not. It is a terror that sits in my chest and waits for me to open that hatch."

Kess did not say it would be fine. She did not say she was sure he could do it. She knew, with the quiet certainty of a root testing soil, that he already knew he could do it. The fear was not a doubt about his ability. It was a fact of his body, a physical reality that no amount of reassurance could erase.

"Okay," she said.

Lio blinked. "Okay?"

"Okay," she repeated. "You are afraid. That is a variable. Let us work with it."
pages.image: Lio, with olive skin and wavy dark hair, sits on a rooftop edge looking at his hands with a worried expression, while Kess, with warm tan skin and a silver hair streak, sits beside him listening intently, the dark curve of the station interior and stars visible above.

pages.text:
Kess fished a stub of pencil from her tool-belt and a scrap of cardboard from her pocket, laying the two on the metal grating between them as if setting out grafting wax. She began to draw lines, her movements brisk and practical, turning the abstract terror into a diagram.

"The fear is the unknown," she said, tapping the pencil tip against the board. "So we make it known. We turn the mystery into a list. A checklist. You do not trust the vacuum, Lio. You trust the procedure. You trust the steps."

She drew a circle. "One. Three points of contact. You never have fewer than three points touching a surface, a rail, or a frame. Two. Tether clipped before unclip. Always clip, then let go. Never let go, then clip. Three. Say each step aloud. You narrate your own actions. If you are silent, your mind can wander into the dark. If you are speaking, you are here."

Lio watched the lines appear, his elbows resting on his knees as he leaned forward. "What if I forget?"

"Then you stop," Kess said, firm and final. "You stop. You do not move. You call for help. You do not guess. You do not improvise. You stop, and you wait, and you listen. That is the fourth rule. Stop."

She drew a square around the circle, enclosing the lines in a small, sturdy frame. "We build a cage for the fear. A small, sturdy cage made of rules. And you stay inside it."

Lio looked at the cardboard, his gaze tracing the geometric boundaries she had just constructed. He reached out and touched the tip of the pencil, but did not take it from her hand, just holding it there while she drew the final line. His shoulders, which had been hunched tight against his ears, began to lower, inch by inch, settling into a position that felt less like defense and more like readiness.

"The cage," he said, his voice softer now. "It sounds like a plan."

"It is a plan," Kess said. "It is the only kind of plan that works in space."
pages.image: Kess draws a circle and square on a piece of cardboard with a pencil, while Lio, in a navy jumpsuit, leans forward watching her with a focused and hopeful expression, the rooftop and festival lights blurring in the background.

pages.text:
A soft green glow bloomed at the edge of the roof. Pim Okafor stood there, balancing on the narrow ledge with the casual grace of a cat that had never learned to fear gravity. His red hooded sweatshirt was bright in the dimness, and his mismatched socks, one blue and one yellow, dangled over the void. In his left hand he held a box of biscuits, and in his right, a bag of sugar that clinked softly against the metal.

"I heard you talking about lists," Pim said, his voice muffled by the cardboard lid of the box. "I have a list. It has forty-one items. It is about biscuits."

Lio looked at the box, then at Kess. He picked up the pencil from the grating and wrote the first item on the scrap of cardboard. His handwriting was neat and precise, the kind that made engineers weep with joy. Kess added the second. Pim added the third, which was about "not dropping the sugar in the vacuum," a concern that seemed entirely reasonable given the physics of free-falling granules.

They sat there for an hour. The spin-gravity tugged gently at their backs. Below them, the festival noise swelled and faded, a distant, rhythmic roar that sounded like the ship’s own breathing. They built the checklist, line by line, word by word. They argued about the order of operations. Pim insisted that "checking the oxygen" should come before "checking the tether." Kess refuted him with a diagram drawn in the air. They debated the best way to phrase the rule about stopping.

"Stop," Kess said. "Just that word. No explanation. No question mark."

"But what if the valve is stuck?" Pim asked.

"Then you stop," Kess said. "And wait."

They laughed, a low, quiet sound that was lost in the hum of the pumps, the tick of the valves, and the steady, inexorable rotation of the drum.

When they were finished, the cardboard was covered in a dense forest of small, careful notes. Lio folded it and tucked it into his breast pocket, smoothing the fabric over it as if it were a precious artifact. He stood up, stretching his legs. For the first time that day, he laughed. It was a real laugh, full and warm, and it echoed in the small space above the street.

"I think," he said, tapping the pocket where the list lived, "we have solved the equation."

Kess smiled, watching him. The fear was still there. It sat in his chest like a knot in a log. But it was no longer a storm that could capsize the ship. It was a weather pattern, predictable and manageable. And they had learned to read it, just like the thermal maps, just like the power budgets, just like the trees.
pages.image: Pim, a boy with two puffs of black hair and a red sweatshirt, stands on a rooftop ledge holding a box of biscuits, while Kess and Lio sit together on the roof, smiling and looking at a piece of cardboard, the festival lights glowing softly around them.

pages.text:
They stood up to go. The roof was slick with the humidity of the festival, a fine mist that had condensed on the metal grating from the warm breath of four thousand people below. Kess’s sneakers, white and stained with the dust of the Orchard, gripped the surface for two steps before the rubber lost its purchase. She slipped, her heel catching on a rivet, and her center of gravity swung outward toward the void.

Lio did not shout. He did not call for help. He simply reached out, his fingers finding the wrist of her tool-belt strap with the precise, practiced ease of a man who had checked his tethers a hundred times in the simulator. He pulled, gently but with absolute certainty, and her feet found the grating again. The movement was small, a correction no larger than adjusting a graft, but the air between them changed.

His grip remained on her wrist for a moment longer than physics required. His fingers were warm and dry, the skin roughened by calluses from the EVA suit’s control panel, and the contact was solid, unyielding, like the steel of a valve handle that would not bend. He held her as she crossed the remaining distance to the door, his hand a steady point of reference in the dark. When they reached the safety of the interior, where the air was dry and smelled faintly of ozone and old paper, he did not let go at once.

They stood there, his hand still holding hers, the amber light of the lamp-panel pulsing softly between them, a warm, rhythmic glow that matched the slow tick of the coolant pumps in the wall.

They both looked at the hand. Then they both looked politely at the stars, which were visible through the glass panel above them, bright and endless and cold, indifferent to the small, warm mess of two people on a ship.

“That’s the best checklist item yet,” Kess said, her voice light, teasing, though it wavered on the last syllable.

Lio looked at her, his dark eyes serious and bright, reflecting the amber light in two small, steady points. “I’m adding it,” he said.

He let go of her hand. He turned and walked toward the door, his steps steady, his shoulders relaxed, the cardboard checklist tucked safely in his breast pocket, a fragile map of their survival. Kess watched him go, the fear in her chest no longer a storm that could capsize the ship, but a weather pattern, predictable and manageable. She followed him, her heart beating a steady, strong rhythm against her ribs, keeping time with the inexorable rotation of the drum.

The ship hummed around them, a vast, living thing, keeping its secrets, keeping its balance. And Kess felt that the balance was holding.
pages.image: Lio, in a navy jumpsuit, holds Kess's hand as she crosses a narrow rail on a rooftop, both looking at the stars through a glass panel, the amber glow of a lamp panel illuminating their faces in the dark.
